1: # conflayers
2: 
3: A configuration loader with no dependencies. It reads INI files, knows a fixed schema of settings, and answers what one of them is set to.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/ini.js` | the INI grammar and the refusals it words, as `IniError`, each with a line and a column |
11: | `src/schema.js` | `SETTINGS`, the known settings with their declared type and default text |
12: | `src/layer.js` | `merge`, which stacks layers so that the last one to set a key wins |
13: 
14: `test/conflayers.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the INI files the examples name.
15: 
16: ## The INI grammar
17: 
18: A line is trimmed first. An empty one, and one beginning with `#` or `;`, is ignored. `[name]` opens a section, and a section may be opened more than once. Anything else is `key = value`: the text before the first `=` is the key, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A key outside a section keeps its own name; a key inside one is prefixed with the section name and a dot, so `port` under `[server]` is `server.port`. A name and a key are one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. Nothing inside a value is special: `#` and `;` open a comment only at the start of a line.
19: 
20: ```ini
21: log.file = /var/log/app.log
22: 
23: [server]
24: port = 9090
25: ```
26: 
27: ## The schema
28: 
29: | Key | Type | Default |
30: | --- | --- | --- |
31: | `log.file` | string | (empty) |
32: | `log.level` | enum `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` | `info` |
33: | `log.rotate` | boolean | `true` |
34: | `retry.attempts` | integer | `3` |
35: | `retry.backoff` | duration | `250ms` |
36: | `server.host` | string | `localhost` |
37: | `server.port` | integer | `8080` |
38: | `server.timeout` | duration | `30s` |
39: | `server.tls` | boolean | `false` |
40: | `tags` | list | (empty) |
41: 
42: The types are declared but nothing here enforces them yet: every mode below prints the raw text as the file wrote it.
43: 
44: ## Modes
45: 
46: - `dump <file>` prints `<key>=<raw text>` for every schema key in ascending order, falling back to the schema default for a key the file leaves out. A key the schema does not know is ignored.
47: - `get <file> <key>` prints the raw text of one setting, or its default. A key outside the schema is refused.
48: 
49: ## Failures
50: 
51: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure carries the position it was read at, as `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: <message>`, where the column counts characters of the raw line from 1, leading whitespace included. The messages are `expected "]"`, reported one past the line's last non-space character; `expected a section name` and `invalid section name <name>`, at the name's first character; `expected a section header or key = value` and `invalid key <key>`, at the line's first non-space character; `expected a key`, at the `=`; and `key <key> is set twice`, at the line's first non-space character. A file that cannot be read is refused as `error: cannot read <path>`, an unknown key as `error: unknown setting <key>`, and a malformed argument list with the usage line.
52: 
53: ## Known gaps
54: 
55: Only one file is ever read, so the `merge` primitive stacks a single layer and nothing overrides anything. Nothing reads the environment. The declared types do nothing: `server.port = eighty` loads as happily as `server.port = 80`, and a caller has to coerce the text itself. `IniError` carries a position, but the parse result does not, so nothing downstream could say where a bad value was written.

1: /** The settings this loader knows, their types, and the text each one defaults to. */
2: 
3: /** Every known setting, in ascending key order. */
4: export const SETTINGS = [
5:   { key: 'log.file', type: 'string', default: '' },
6:   { key: 'log.level', type: 'enum', members: ['debug', 'info', 'warn', 'error'], default: 'info' },
7:   { key: 'log.rotate', type: 'boolean', default: 'true' },
8:   { key: 'retry.attempts', type: 'integer', default: '3' },
9:   { key: 'retry.backoff', type: 'duration', default: '250ms' },
10:   { key: 'server.host', type: 'string', default: 'localhost' },
11:   { key: 'server.port', type: 'integer', default: '8080' },
12:   { key: 'server.timeout', type: 'duration', default: '30s' },
13:   { key: 'server.tls', type: 'boolean', default: 'false' },
14:   { key: 'tags', type: 'list', default: '' },
15: ]
16: 
17: const BY_KEY = new Map(SETTINGS.map(declared => [declared.key, declared]))
18: 
19: /**
20:  * The setting one key names, or undefined when the schema does not know it.
21:  * @param {string} key - the dotted setting key.
22:  * @returns {{key: string, type: string, members?: string[], default: string} | undefined} the setting.
23:  */
24: export function setting(key) {
25:   return BY_KEY.get(key)
26: }
27: 
28: const INTEGER = /^-?(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)$/
29: const DURATION = /^([0-9]+)(ms|s|m|h)$/
30: const UNIT_MS = { ms: 1, s: 1000, m: 60_000, h: 3_600_000 }
31: 
32: /** One value the schema refuses, worded without the position the caller adds. */
33: export class ValueError extends Error {
34:   /**
35:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
36:    */
37:   constructor(message) {
38:     super(message)
39:     this.name = 'ValueError'
40:   }
41: }
42: 
43: /** The items of a list value, trimmed, first occurrence kept. */
44: function items(declared, text) {
45:   throw new Error('not implemented')
46: }
47: 
48: /**
49:  * Coerce one setting's text and render it the way `load` prints it.
50:  * @param {{key: string, type: string, members?: string[]}} declared - the setting the text belongs to.
51:  * @param {string} text - the raw text the winning layer wrote.
52:  * @returns {string} the canonical rendering.
53:  * @throws {ValueError} when the text does not fit the declared type.
54:  */
55: export function coerce(declared, text) {
56:   switch (declared.type) {
57:     case 'integer':
58:       if (!INTEGER.test(text)) throw new ValueError(`${declared.key} is not an integer: ${text}`)
59:       return text
60:     case 'boolean':
61:       if (text !== 'true' && text !== 'false') throw new ValueError(`${declared.key} is not a boolean: ${text}`)
62:       return text
63:     case 'enum':
64:       if (!declared.members.includes(text)) {
65:         throw new ValueError(`${declared.key} is not one of ${declared.members.join('|')}: ${text}`)
66:       }
67:       return text
68:     case 'duration': {
69:       const match = DURATION.exec(text)
70:       if (match === null) throw new ValueError(`${declared.key} is not a duration: ${text}`)
71:       return String(Number(match[1]) * UNIT_MS[match[2]])
72:     }
73:     case 'list':
74:       return items(declared, text).join(',')
75:     default:
76:       return text
77:   }
78: }

1: #!/usr/bin/env node
2: /** The command: `dump <file>`, `get <file> <key>`, `load <base> <site>` and `origin <base> <site>`. */
3: 
4: import { existsSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
5: import { EnvError, parse as parseEnv } from './env.js'
6: import { IniError, parse as parseIni } from './ini.js'
7: import { merge } from './layer.js'
8: import { coerce, SETTINGS, setting, ValueError } from './schema.js'
9: 
10: const USAGE = 'usage: cli.js dump <file>|get <file> <key>|load <base> <site>|origin <base> <site>'
11: 
12: /** Report one failure the way the specification words it, and stop. */
13: function fail(message) {
14:   process.stderr.write(`error: ${message}\n`)
15:   process.exit(2)
16: }
17: 
18: /** One INI layer, refused at its own position when the grammar or the schema rejects it. */
19: function iniLayer(name, path, strict) {
20:   if (!existsSync(path)) fail(`cannot read ${path}`)
21:   let values
22:   try {
23:     values = parseIni(readFileSync(path, 'utf8'))
24:   } catch (error) {
25:     if (!(error instanceof IniError)) throw error
26:     fail(`${path}:${error.line}:${error.column}: ${error.message}`)
27:   }
28:   if (strict) {
29:     for (const [key, value] of values) {
30:       if (setting(key) === undefined) fail(`${path}:${value.line}:${value.column}: unknown setting ${key}`)
31:     }
32:   }
33:   return { name, values }
34: }
35: 
36: /** The environment layer, refused at its own position. */
37: function envLayer() {
38:   try {
39:     return { name: 'env', values: parseEnv(readFileSync(0, 'utf8'), SETTINGS) }
40:   } catch (error) {
41:     if (!(error instanceof EnvError)) throw error
42:     return fail(`<stdin>:${error.line}:${error.column}: ${error.message}`)
43:   }
44: }
45: 
46: const argv = process.argv.slice(2)
47: const mode = argv[0]
48: const arity = { dump: 2, get: 3, load: 3, origin: 3 }
49: if (argv.length !== arity[mode]) fail(USAGE)
50: 
51: const out = []
52: if (mode === 'dump' || mode === 'get') {
53:   const { values } = iniLayer('file', argv[1], false)
54:   const raw = key => (values.has(key) ? values.get(key).text : setting(key).default)
55:   if (mode === 'dump') {
56:     for (const declared of SETTINGS) out.push(`${declared.key}=${raw(declared.key)}`)
57:   } else {
58:     if (setting(argv[2]) === undefined) fail(`unknown setting ${argv[2]}`)
59:     out.push(raw(argv[2]))
60:   }
61: } else {
62:   const merged = merge([iniLayer('base', argv[1], true), iniLayer('site', argv[2], true), envLayer()])
63:   const source = { base: argv[1], site: argv[2], env: '<stdin>' }
64:   for (const declared of SETTINGS) {
65:     const won = merged.get(declared.key)
66:     if (mode === 'origin') {
67:       out.push(`${declared.key} ${won === undefined ? 'default' : won.name}`)
68:       continue
69:     }
70:     if (won === undefined) {
71:       out.push(`${declared.key}=${coerce(declared, declared.default)}`)
72:       continue

`conflayers` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/conflayers.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the two layered modes its `merge` primitive was built for, make the declared types real, and report a bad value where it was written. Everything `README.md` documents about `dump`, `get`, the INI grammar and the existing failures stays exactly as it is, including every message and every column; the work spans the parser, the schema, the layer stack, and the command.

`load <base> <site>` and `origin <base> <site>` each stack three layers, weakest first: the INI file named by the first argument, the INI file named by the second, and an environment layer read from standard input. A later layer overrides a key an earlier one set, one key at a time, so a file that sets only `server.port` leaves every other key to the layer below it. The layers are read in that order, and a layer's failures are all reported before the next layer is read.

The environment layer is a line per variable. A line is trimmed first; an empty one, and one beginning with `#`, is ignored. The rest is `NAME=VALUE`: the text before the first `=` is the name, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A setting travels under `CONF_` followed by its key uppercased with every `.` replaced by `_`, so `server.port` arrives as `CONF_SERVER_PORT`. Its failures carry a position too, worded `error: <stdin>:<line>:<column>: ` followed by `expected NAME=VALUE` or `expected a variable name` or `unknown environment variable <NAME>` or `<NAME> is set twice`, each reported at the line's first non-space character and each counting columns the way the INI parser does.

Both modes are strict about keys where `dump` is lenient: a key an INI layer sets and the schema does not know fails with `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: unknown setting <key>` at the value's position, and a layer's keys are checked in the order the file writes them, after that file parses. The value's position is the column of its first character, or, when the value is empty, one past the line's last non-space character.

`origin <base> <site>` prints `<key> <layer>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the layer is `base`, `site`, `env`, or `default` when no layer set the key.

`load <base> <site>` prints `<key>=<value>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the value is the winning layer's text coerced by the key's declared type, or the schema default coerced the same way. A `string` is its text. An `integer` is an optional `-` and then digits without a leading zero, unless the number is exactly `0`, and renders as written. A `boolean` is `true` or `false`, lowercase, and renders as written. An `enum` is one of its declared members and renders as written. A `duration` is digits followed by `ms`, `s`, `m` or `h`, and renders as its whole number of milliseconds. A `list` is items separated by commas, each trimmed, with a repeat dropped and the order kept, rendered joined by single commas; empty text is the empty list and renders empty, but an empty item between two commas is a failure. A value that does not fit its type fails with `error: <where>: <message>`, where `<where>` is the file and position it was written at, or `<stdin>` and its position when the environment layer set it, and the message is `<key> is not an integer: <text>`, `<key> is not a boolean: <text>`, `<key> is not one of <members joined by |>: <text>`, `<key> is not a duration: <text>` or `<key> has an empty item: <text>`. The keys are coerced in ascending order, so the first failing key in that order decides.

The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js dump <file>|get <file> <key>|load <base> <site>|origin <base> <site>`; `dump` takes one path, `get` a path and a key, and `load` and `origin` exactly two paths.

Add the retry policy the simulator was built around, somewhere for a job that never succeeds to go, and a way to run one log under a policy that does not live in it. Everything `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is — the log grammar, the simulation, the `trace` and `summary` output, and every failure message and exit code — and the work spans the parser, the simulation, and the command.

`retry <max> <base>` joins the log's directives, parsed like `limit`: exactly two words after it, `<max>` a positive integer and `<base>` a non-negative one, at most one such line, and the same failures as the others, worded `expected retry <max> <base>`, `max must be a positive integer`, `base must be a non-negative integer` and `retry is declared twice`. The directive turns the policy on. With no `retry` line anywhere a job still gets one attempt and a failure is simply final, exactly as today.

Under a retry policy, an attempt that finishes `fail` goes back in the queue when its attempt number is below `<max>`, ready at the instant it failed plus `<base>` multiplied by two raised to the power of one less than that attempt number, so the first backoff is `<base>`, the second twice that, the third four times. A re-queued attempt competes for the worker like any other: it is taken when its ready time is the smallest, ties still break by submission order, and its start still waits out the rate limit. An attempt that finishes `fail` at attempt `<max>` is dead-lettered instead, at the instant it failed.

`dead` is a new mode. It prints one line per dead-lettered job in the order the jobs were written off, `<id> attempts=<n> at=<instant>`, and then a final line `total <k>` counting them. In `summary`, a dead-lettered job reads `dead` in place of its last attempt's outcome; every other job reads that outcome as before.

Every mode takes an optional second argument naming a policy file, so the usage line becomes `error: usage: cli.js trace|summary|dead [<policy>]`. A policy file holds `limit` and `retry` lines and nothing else, read under the log's own grammar, with a line trimmed and an empty one or one starting with `#` ignored. It is read before the log, so its failures come first, and a directive it sets is already in force when the log is parsed: a log that sets the same directive fails at the log's own line with `limit is declared twice` or `retry is declared twice`. A policy file's own failures are worded `error: <policy>: line N: ` followed by the message the same directive would give in the log, with `unknown directive <word>` for anything that is not `limit` or `retry`, and N counting the policy file's own lines from 1. 1: # jobq
2: 
3: A job-queue simulator with no dependencies. It reads a log from standard input and replays it on one worker against a clock that only moves when the simulation asks it to, so a run is the same on every machine and in every order.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/parse.js` | the log grammar and the refusals it words, as `LogError` |
11: | `src/queue.js` | the simulation: what starts when, and what the rate limit holds back |
12: | `src/clock.js` | `createClock`, the monotonic clock the simulation advances by hand |
13: 
14: `test/jobq.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the policy files the examples name.
15: 
16: ## The log
17: 
18: One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace. Every number is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign or a separator.
19: 
20: ```
21: limit 2 10
22: job build 5 ok
23: job flaky 3 fail ok
24: submit 0 build
25: submit 0 flaky
26: ```
27: 
28: `limit <starts> <window>` allows at most `<starts>` starts inside any window of `<window>` milliseconds, and may appear at most once. `job <id> <duration> <outcome>...` declares a job that occupies the worker for `<duration>` milliseconds and whose attempts turn out as the listed `ok` and `fail` words, the last of which repeats. An id is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. `submit <at> <id>` puts a declared job in the queue at that instant; a job may be submitted at most once.
29: 
30: ## The simulation
31: 
32: The clock starts at 0 and one worker runs everything. Take the queued attempt with the smallest ready time, breaking ties by submission order, and advance the clock to that ready time. If a rate limit is in force and the last `<starts>` starts all fall inside the window ending now, advance the clock to the instant the oldest of them leaves it. The attempt starts at the clock's instant and finishes `<duration>` later, and the clock advances to that finish. A job of duration 0 finishes in the instant it starts. A failed attempt is simply over: nothing here retries it.
33: 
34: ## Modes
35: 
36: - `trace` prints one line per attempt in the order the attempts started, `<start> <id> attempt=<n> <outcome> finish=<finish>`, and then a final `end <clock>` line.
37: - `summary` prints one line per submitted job in ascending id order, `<id> attempts=<n> <outcome of its last attempt>`, and then the same final `end <clock>` line.
38: 
39: A declared job nothing submits never runs and appears nowhere.
40: 
41: ## Failures
42: 
43: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure names its 1-based log line: `error: line 2: unknown directive cancel`. The messages are `expected limit <starts> <window>`, `expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...`, `expected submit <at> <id>`, `invalid job id <id>`, `invalid outcome <word>`, `<field> must be a non-negative integer` and `<field> must be a positive integer` naming `at`, `duration`, `starts` or `window`, `job <id> is declared twice`, `job <id> is submitted twice`, `limit is declared twice`, and `unknown directive <word>`. A `submit` line naming a job no `job` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown job <id>`. A malformed argument list is refused with the usage line.
44: 
45: ## Known gaps
46: 
47: A failure is the end of a job: there is no retry, no backoff, and nowhere for a job that never succeeds to go. The rate limit and nothing else can be configured, it can only come from the log itself, and there is no way to run the same log under a different policy.

30: /** One field read as a non-negative integer, or the failure that names it. */
31: function count(line, field, word) {

33:   return Number(word)
34: }
35: 
36: /** One field read as a positive integer, or the failure that names it. */
37: function positive(line, field, word) {

54:     if (policy.limit !== undefined) throw new LogError(line, 'limit is declared twice')
55:     policy.limit = { starts: positive(line, 'starts', words[1]), window: positive(line, 'window', words[2]) }

57:   }
58:   if (words[0] === 'retry') {

60:     if (policy.retry !== undefined) throw new LogError(line, 'retry is declared twice')
61:     policy.retry = { max: positive(line, 'max', words[1]), base: count(line, 'base', words[2]) }

1: /** The simulation: one worker, a rate limit on starts, and a retry policy with backoff. */
2: 
3: import { createClock } from './clock.js'
4: 
5: /**
6:  * Run every submission to a verdict.
7:  * @param {Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>} jobs - the declared jobs.
8:  * @param {{id: string, at: number}[]} submissions - the submissions, in input order.
9:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}, retry?: {max: number, base: number}}} policy - the rate limit and retry policy in force.
10:  * @returns {{attempts: {start: number, id: string, attempt: number, outcome: string, finish: number}[], dead: {id: string, attempts: number, at: number}[], end: number}} the attempts in the order they started, the dead letters in the order they were written off, and the clock at the end.
11:  */
12: export function run(jobs, submissions, policy) {
13:   const clock = createClock()
14:   const queued = submissions.map((submission, order) => ({ ...submission, order, readyAt: submission.at, attempt: 0 }))
15:   const attempts = []
16:   const dead = []
17:   const starts = []
18:   const maxAttempts = policy.retry === undefined ? 1 : policy.retry.max
19:   while (queued.length > 0) {
20:     let pick = 0
21:     for (const [index, entry] of queued.entries()) {
22:       const best = queued[pick]
23:       if (entry.readyAt < best.readyAt || (entry.readyAt === best.readyAt && entry.order < best.order)) pick = index
24:     }
25:     const entry = queued.splice(pick, 1)[0]
26:     clock.advanceTo(entry.readyAt)
27:     if (policy.limit !== undefined && starts.length >= policy.limit.starts) {
28:       const oldest = starts[starts.length - policy.limit.starts]
29:       if (clock.now() - oldest < policy.limit.window) clock.advanceTo(oldest + policy.limit.window)
30:     }
31:     const job = jobs.get(entry.id)
32:     const start = clock.now()
33:     starts.push(start)
34:     const attempt = entry.attempt + 1
35:     const outcome = job.outcomes[Math.min(attempt, job.outcomes.length) - 1]
36:     const finish = start + job.duration
37:     clock.advanceTo(finish)
38:     attempts.push({ start, id: entry.id, attempt, outcome, finish })
39:     if (outcome === 'fail' && policy.retry !== undefined) {
40:       if (attempt < maxAttempts) {
41:         queued.push({ ...entry, attempt, readyAt: finish + policy.retry.base * 2 ** (attempt - 1) })
42:       } else {
43:         dead.push({ id: entry.id, attempts: attempt, at: finish })
44:       }
45:     }
46:   }
47:   return { attempts, dead, end: clock.now() }
48: }

Everything `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is — the log grammar, the simulation, the `trace` and `summary` output, and every failure message and exit code — and the work spans the parser, the simulation, and the command.

`retry <max> <base>` joins the log's directives, parsed like `limit`: exactly two words after it, `<max>` a positive integer and `<base>` a non-negative one, at most one such line, and the same failures as the others, worded `expected retry <max> <base>`, `max must be a positive integer`, `base must be a non-negative integer` and `retry is declared twice`. The directive turns the policy on. With no `retry` line anywhere a job still gets one attempt and a failure is simply final, exactly as today.

Under a retry policy, an attempt that finishes `fail` goes back in the queue when its attempt number is below `<max>`, ready at the instant it failed plus `<base>` multiplied by two raised to the power of one less than that attempt number, so the first backoff is `<base>`, the second twice that, the third four times. A re-queued attempt competes for the worker like any other: it is taken when its ready time is the smallest, ties still break by submission order, and its start still waits out the rate limit. An attempt that finishes `fail` at attempt `<max>` is dead-lettered instead, at the instant it failed.

`dead` is a new mode. It prints one line per dead-lettered job in the order the jobs were written off, `<id> attempts=<n> at=<instant>`, and then a final line `total <k>` counting them. In `summary`, a dead-lettered job reads `dead` in place of its last attempt's outcome; every other job reads that outcome as before.

Every mode takes an optional second argument naming a policy file, so the usage line becomes `error: usage: cli.js trace|summary|dead [<policy>]`. A policy file holds `limit` and `retry` lines and nothing else, read under the log's own grammar, with a line trimmed and an empty one or one starting with `#` ignored. It is read before the log, so its failures come first, and a directive it sets is already in force when the log is parsed: a log that sets the same directive fails at the log's own line with `limit is declared twice` or `retry is declared twice`. A policy file's own failures are worded `error: <policy>: line N: ` followed by the message the same directive would give in the log, with `unknown directive <word>` for anything that is not `limit` or `retry`, and N counting the policy file's own lines from 1. A policy file that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read policy <path>`.

`taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.

Two directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.

`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.

A task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. A task no watched path condemns runs anyway when some dependency runs, with the reason `needs <dep>` naming the lexicographically smallest dependency that runs, so a path reason always wins over a dependency one. `plan` prints one line per task in the order `order` prints, `run <name> <reason>` or `skip <name>`, and then a final line `total run=<r> skip=<s>` counting the two.

1: # taskrun
2: 
3: A dependency-aware task runner with no dependencies of its own. It reads a task file from standard input and answers questions about it; it never executes a command.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/parse.js` | the task-file grammar and the refusals it words, as `ParseError` |
11: | `src/graph.js` | run order over the dependency edges |
12: | `src/digest.js` | the FNV-1a digest the snapshot format records |
13: 
14: `test/taskrun.test.js` is the suite for what is already here. `data/files/` holds the workspace files the examples name, and `data/snapshots/` the digest snapshots.
15: 
16: ## The task file
17: 
18: One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace.
19: 
20: ```
21: # build.tasks
22: task build node build.js
23: task bundle node bundle.js
24: needs bundle build
25: ```
26: 
27: `task <name> <word>...` declares a task whose command is the remaining words joined with single spaces. `needs <name> <dependency>...` adds dependencies; a repeated edge counts once, and a `needs` line may stand before the `task` line it names.
28: 
29: ## Modes
30: 
31: - `order` prints the task names one per line, in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose dependencies have all been printed.
32: - `show <name>` prints `<name>: <command>` and then `needs: ` followed by the dependencies in ascending order, or `-` when there are none.
33: - `digest <path>...` prints `<path> <digest>` for each path in argument order, with `missing` in place of a digest for a path that is not there. The digest is 32-bit FNV-1a over the file's bytes — offset basis `0x811c9dc5`, prime `16777619`, xor then multiply — as eight lowercase hex digits.
34: 
35: ## Failures
36: 
37: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A parse failure names its 1-based input line: `error: line 2: unknown directive run`. The messages are `expected task <name> <word>...`, `expected needs <name> <dependency>...`, `invalid task name <name>`, `task <name> is declared twice` and `unknown directive <word>`. A `needs` line naming a task no `task` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown task <name>`, and so is `show` on such a name.
38: 
39: ## Known gaps
40: 
41: `order` does not detect a dependency cycle: it stops as soon as nothing is ready and leaves every task in the cycle out of its output. The task file has no way to declare which files a task reads or writes, so nothing here can tell whether a task is up to date.

1: /** Ordering the task graph, and naming the cycle that stops it. */
2: 
3: /** A dependency cycle, carrying the names that close it. */
4: export class CycleError extends Error {
5:   /**
6:    * @param {string[]} names - the cycle from the re-entered task back to itself, the repeat included.
7:    */
8:   constructor(names) {
9:     super(`cycle: ${names.join(' -> ')}`)
10:     this.name = 'CycleError'
11:     this.names = names
12:   }
13: }
14: 
15: /**
16:  * The cycle a depth-first search finds first, or undefined when the graph is acyclic.
17:  * The search starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's
18:  * dependencies in ascending name order; the cycle runs from the task the search
19:  * re-entered, through the stack, back to that task.
20:  * @param {Map<string, {needs: string[]}>} tasks - the parsed tasks.
21:  * @returns {string[] | undefined} the cycle's names, the repeat included.
22:  */
23: export function findCycle(tasks) {
24:   const names = [...tasks.keys()].sort()
25:   const done = new Set()
26:   const stack = []
27:   const onStack = new Set()
28:   const walk = (name) => {
29:     if (onStack.has(name)) return [...stack.slice(stack.indexOf(name)), name]
30:     if (done.has(name)) return undefined
31:     stack.push(name)
32:     onStack.add(name)
33:     for (const need of [...tasks.get(name).needs].sort()) {
34:       const found = walk(need)
35:       if (found !== undefined) return found
36:     }
37:     stack.pop()
38:     onStack.delete(name)
39:     done.add(name)
40:     return undefined
41:   }
42:   for (const name of names) {
43:     const found = walk(name)
44:     if (found !== undefined) return found
45:   }
46:   return undefined
47: }
48: 
49: /**
50:  * The tasks in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose
51:  * dependencies have all been emitted.
52:  * @param {Map<string, {needs: string[]}>} tasks - the parsed tasks.
53:  * @returns {string[]} the names in run order.
54:  * @throws {CycleError} when a dependency cycle leaves the order undefined.
55:  */
56: export function order(tasks) {
57:   const cycle = findCycle(tasks)
58:   if (cycle !== undefined) throw new CycleError(cycle)
59:   const remaining = new Set(tasks.keys())
60:   const emitted = new Set()
61:   const out = []
62:   while (remaining.size > 0) {
63:     const ready = [...remaining].filter(name => tasks.get(name).needs.every(need => emitted.has(need))).sort()
64:     const next = ready[0]
65:     remaining.delete(next)
66:     emitted.add(next)
67:     out.push(next)
68:   }
69:   return out
70: }

1: /** The snapshot reader and the staleness rule that decides what a plan runs. */
2: 
3: import { existsSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
4: import { digestBytes } from './digest.js'
5: import { order } from './graph.js'
6: 
7: const DIGEST = /^[0-9a-f]{8}$/
8: 
9: /** One refusal of a snapshot file, carrying the file and the 1-based line. */
10: export class SnapshotError extends Error {
11:   /**
12:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the `error: ` prefix.
13:    */
14:   constructor(message) {
15:     super(message)
16:     this.name = 'SnapshotError'
17:   }
18: }
19: 
20: /**
21:  * Read one snapshot file into the digests it records.
22:  * @param {string} path - the snapshot's workspace path, as the argument gave it.
23:  * @returns {Map<string, string>} the recorded digest of each path.
24:  * @throws {SnapshotError} when the file is unreadable or a line is malformed.
25:  */
26: export function readSnapshot(path) {
27:   if (!existsSync(path)) throw new SnapshotError(`cannot read snapshot ${path}`)
28:   const recorded = new Map()
29:   const lines = readFileSync(path, 'utf8').split('\n')
30:   if (lines.length > 0 && lines[lines.length - 1] === '') lines.pop()
31:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
32:     const line = index + 1
33:     const text = raw.trim()
34:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
35:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
36:     if (words.length !== 2) throw new SnapshotError(`${path}: line ${line}: expected <path> <digest>`)
37:     if (!DIGEST.test(words[1])) throw new SnapshotError(`${path}: line ${line}: invalid digest ${words[1]}`)
38:     if (recorded.has(words[0])) throw new SnapshotError(`${path}: line ${line}: path ${words[0]} is recorded twice`)
39:     recorded.set(words[0], words[1])
40:   }
41:   return recorded
42: }
43: 
44: /**
45:  * Why one watched path makes its task stale, or undefined when it does not.
46:  * @param {string} path - the watched workspace path.
47:  * @param {Map<string, string>} recorded - the snapshot's digests.
48:  * @returns {string | undefined} the reason, as the plan line words it.
49:  */
50: function pathReason(path, recorded) {
51:   if (!recorded.has(path)) return `new ${path}`
52:   if (!existsSync(path)) return `missing ${path}`
53:   return digestBytes(readFileSync(path)) === recorded.get(path) ? undefined : `changed ${path}`
54: }
55: 
56: /**
57:  * Decide, for every task in run order, whether the plan runs it and why.
58:  * @param {Map<string, {needs: string[], reads: string[], writes: string[]}>} tasks - the parsed tasks.
59:  * @param {Map<string, string>} recorded - the snapshot's digests.
60:  * @returns {{name: string, reason: string | undefined}[]} one decision per task, in run order.
61:  */
62: export function plan(tasks, recorded) {
63:   const running = new Set()
64:   return order(tasks).map((name) => {
65:     const task = tasks.get(name)
66:     const watched = [...new Set([...task.reads, ...task.writes])].sort()
67:     let reason
68:     for (const path of watched) {
69:       reason = pathReason(path, recorded)
70:       if (reason !== undefined) break
71:     }
72:     if (reason === undefined) {
73:       const stale = [...task.needs].sort().find(need => running.has(need))
74:       if (stale !== undefined) reason = `needs ${stale}`
75:     }
76:     if (reason !== undefined) running.add(name)
77:     return { name, reason }
78:   })
79: }

1: /** FNV-1a over raw bytes, the digest the snapshot format records. */
2: 
3: const OFFSET = 0x811c9dc5
4: const PRIME = 16777619
5: 
6: /**
7:  * The 32-bit FNV-1a digest of a byte buffer as eight lowercase hex digits.
8:  * @param {Buffer} bytes - the bytes to digest.
9:  * @returns {string} the digest.
10:  */
11: export function digestBytes(bytes) {
12:   let hash = OFFSET >>> 0
13:   for (const byte of bytes) {
14:     hash = (hash ^ byte) >>> 0
15:     hash = Math.imul(hash, PRIME) >>> 0
16:   }
17:   return hash.toString(16).padStart(8, '0')
18: }

`taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.

Two directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.

`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.

A task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. A task no watched path condemns runs anyway when some dependency runs, with the reason `needs <dep>` naming the lexicographically smallest dependency that runs, so a path reason always wins over a dependency one. `plan` prints one line per task in the order `order` prints, `run <name> <reason>` or `skip <name>`, and then a final line `total run=<r> skip=<s>` counting the two.

1: # conflayers
2: 
3: A configuration loader with no dependencies. It reads INI files, knows a fixed schema of settings, and answers what one of them is set to.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/ini.js` | the INI grammar and the refusals it words, as `IniError`, each with a line and a column |
11: | `src/schema.js` | `SETTINGS`, the known settings with their declared type and default text |
12: | `src/layer.js` | `merge`, which stacks layers so that the last one to set a key wins |
13: 
14: `test/conflayers.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the INI files the examples name.
15: 
16: ## The INI grammar
17: 
18: A line is trimmed first. An empty one, and one beginning with `#` or `;`, is ignored. `[name]` opens a section, and a section may be opened more than once. Anything else is `key = value`: the text before the first `=` is the key, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A key outside a section keeps its own name; a key inside one is prefixed with the section name and a dot, so `port` under `[server]` is `server.port`. A name and a key are one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. Nothing inside a value is special: `#` and `;` open a comment only at the start of a line.
19: 
20: ```ini
21: log.file = /var/log/app.log
22: 
23: [server]
24: port = 9090
25: ```
26: 
27: ## The schema
28: 
29: | Key | Type | Default |
30: | --- | --- | --- |
31: | `log.file` | string | (empty) |
32: | `log.level` | enum `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` | `info` |
33: | `log.rotate` | boolean | `true` |
34: | `retry.attempts` | integer | `3` |
35: | `retry.backoff` | duration | `250ms` |
36: | `server.host` | string | `localhost` |
37: | `server.port` | integer | `8080` |
38: | `server.timeout` | duration | `30s` |
39: | `server.tls` | boolean | `false` |
40: | `tags` | list | (empty) |
41: 
42: The types are declared but nothing here enforces them yet: every mode below prints the raw text as the file wrote it.
43: 
44: ## Modes
45: 
46: - `dump <file>` prints `<key>=<raw text>` for every schema key in ascending order, falling back to the schema default for a key the file leaves out. A key the schema does not know is ignored.
47: - `get <file> <key>` prints the raw text of one setting, or its default. A key outside the schema is refused.
48: 
49: ## Failures
50: 
51: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure carries the position it was read at, as `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: <message>`, where the column counts characters of the raw line from 1, leading whitespace included. The messages are `expected "]"`, reported one past the line's last non-space character; `expected a section name` and `invalid section name <name>`, at the name's first character; `expected a section header or key = value` and `invalid key <key>`, at the line's first non-space character; `expected a key`, at the `=`; and `key <key> is set twice`, at the line's first non-space character. A file that cannot be read is refused as `error: cannot read <path>`, an unknown key as `error: unknown setting <key>`, and a malformed argument list with the usage line.
52: 
53: ## Known gaps
54: 
55: Only one file is ever read, so the `merge` primitive stacks a single layer and nothing overrides anything. Nothing reads the environment. The declared types do nothing: `server.port = eighty` loads as happily as `server.port = 80`, and a caller has to coerce the text itself. `IniError` carries a position, but the parse result does not, so nothing downstream could say where a bad value was written.

6:   { key: 'log.level', type: 'enum', members: ['debug', 'info', 'warn', 'error'], default: 'info' },
7:   { key: 'log.rotate', type: 'boolean', default: 'true' },
8:   { key: 'retry.attempts', type: 'integer', default: '3' },

15: ]

17: const BY_KEY = new Map(SETTINGS.map(declared => [declared.key, declared]))

19: /**
20:  * The setting one key names, or undefined when the schema does not know it.

45:   if (text === '') return []
46:   const out = []
47:   for (const item of text.split(',')) {
48:     const trimmed = item.trim()
49:     if (trimmed === '') throw new ValueError(`${declared.key} has an empty item: ${text}`)

70:     case 'enum':

2: 
3: const NAME = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: 
5: /** One refusal of an INI line, carrying the 1-based line and column it was read at. */
6: export class IniError extends Error {
7:   /**
8:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line.
9:    * @param {number} column - the 1-based column of the raw line.
10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, column, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'IniError'
15:     this.line = line
16:     this.column = column
17:   }
18: }
19: 
20: /** The 1-based column of the first non-space character of `raw`. */
21: function indent(raw) {
22:   return raw.length - raw.trimStart().length + 1
23: }
24: 
25: /**
26:  * Parse INI text into its settings.
27:  * @param {string} text - the file's whole text.
28:  * @returns {Map<string, {text: string, line: number, column: number}>} each dotted key's raw value and position, in the order the file writes them.
29:  * @throws {IniError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
30:  */
31: export function parse(text) {
32:   const lines = text.split('\n')
33:   if (lines.length > 0 && lines[lines.length - 1] === '') lines.pop()
34:   const values = new Map()
35:   let section = ''
36:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
37:     const line = index + 1
38:     const trimmed = raw.trim()
39:     if (trimmed === '' || trimmed.startsWith('#') || trimmed.startsWith(';')) continue
40:     if (trimmed.startsWith('[')) {
41:       if (!trimmed.endsWith(']')) throw new IniError(line, raw.trimEnd().length + 1, 'expected "]"')
42:       const name = trimmed.slice(1, -1)
43:       if (name === '') throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + 1, 'expected a section name')
44:       if (!NAME.test(name)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + 1, `invalid section name ${name}`)
45:       section = name
46:       continue
47:     }
48:     const split = trimmed.indexOf('=')
49:     if (split === -1) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), 'expected a section header or key = value')
50:     const key = trimmed.slice(0, split).trim()
51:     if (key === '') throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + split, 'expected a key')
52:     if (!NAME.test(key)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), `invalid key ${key}`)
53:     const full = section === '' ? key : `${section}.${key}`
54:     if (values.has(full)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), `key ${full} is set twice`)
55:     const after = raw.indexOf('=', indent(raw) - 1) + 1
56:     const rest = raw.slice(after)
57:     const column = rest.trim() === '' ? raw.trimEnd().length + 1 : after + (rest.length - rest.trimStart().length) + 1
58:     values.set(full, { text: rest.trim(), line, column })
59:   }
60:   return values
61: }

2: 
3: /**
4:  * Merge named layers, later over earlier.
5:  * @param {readonly {name: string, values: Map<string, {text: string, line: number, column: number}>}[]} layers - the layers, weakest first.
6:  * @returns {Map<string, {name: string, text: string, line: number, column: number}>} each key's winning value, with the layer that set it.
7:  */
8: export function merge(layers) {
9:   const merged = new Map()
10:   for (const layer of layers) {
11:     for (const [key, value] of layer.values) merged.set(key, { name: layer.name, ...value })
12:   }
13:   return merged
14: }

1: /** The environment layer: `NAME=VALUE` lines read from standard input. */
2: 
3: /** One refusal of an environment line, carrying the 1-based line and column. */
4: export class EnvError extends Error {
5:   /**
6:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line.
7:    * @param {number} column - the 1-based column of the raw line.
8:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
9:    */
10:   constructor(line, column, message) {
11:     super(message)
12:     this.name = 'EnvError'
13:     this.line = line
14:     this.column = column
15:   }
16: }
17: 
18: /** The 1-based column of the first non-space character of `raw`. */
19: function indent(raw) {
20:   return raw.length - raw.trimStart().length + 1
21: }
22: 
23: /**
24:  * The variable name one setting key travels under.
25:  * @param {string} key - the dotted setting key.
26:  * @returns {string} the variable name.
27:  */
28: export function variableName(key) {
29:   return `CONF_${key.toUpperCase().replaceAll('.', '_')}`
30: }
31: 
32: /**
33:  * Parse the environment layer.
34:  * @param {string} text - everything standard input carried.
35:  * @param {readonly {key: string}[]} settings - the schema, which decides which names are known.
36:  * @returns {Map<string, {text: string, line: number, column: number}>} each dotted key's raw value and position, in the order the input writes them.
37:  * @throws {EnvError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
38:  */
39: export function parse(text, settings) {
40:   const lines = text.split('\n')
41:   if (lines.length > 0 && lines[lines.length - 1] === '') lines.pop()
42: 
43:   // Create a map of variable names to their corresponding keys
44:   const varToKey = new Map()
45:   for (const setting of settings) {
46:     varToKey.set(variableName(setting.key), setting.key)
47:   }
48: 
49:   const values = new Map()
50: 
51:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
52:     const line = index + 1
53:     const trimmed = raw.trim()
54:     const col = indent(raw) // column position for error reporting
55: 
56:     // Skip empty lines and comments
57:     if (trimmed === '' || trimmed.startsWith('#')) continue
58: 
59:     // Parse NAME=VALUE format
60:     const eqIndexTrimmed = trimmed.indexOf('=')
61:     if (eqIndexTrimmed === -1) {
62:       throw new EnvError(line, col, 'expected NAME=VALUE')
63:     }
64: 
65:     const name = trimmed.slice(0, eqIndexTrimmed).trim()
66:     if (name === '') {
67:       throw new EnvError(line, col, 'expected a variable name')
68:     }
69: 
70:     // Check if the variable name is known
71:     if (!varToKey.has(name)) {
72:       throw new EnvError(line, col, `unknown environment variable ${name}`)
73:     }
74: 
75:     const key = varToKey.get(name)
76: 
77:     // Check for duplicates
78:     if (values.has(key)) {
79:       throw new EnvError(line, col, `${name} is set twice`)
80:     }
81: 
82:     const value = trimmed.slice(eqIndexTrimmed + 1).trim()
83: 
84:     // Calculate column position for the value
85:     const eqIndexRaw = raw.indexOf('=', col - 1)
86:     const after = eqIndexRaw + 1
87:     const rest = raw.slice(after)
88:     const column = rest.trim() === '' ? raw.trimEnd().length + 1 : after + (rest.length - rest.trimStart().length) + 1
89: 
90:     values.set(key, { text: value, line, column })
91:   }
92: 
93:   return values
94: }

1: # conflayers
2: 
3: A configuration loader with no dependencies. It reads INI files, knows a fixed schema of settings, and answers what one of them is set to.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/ini.js` | the INI grammar and the refusals it words, as `IniError`, each with a line and a column |
11: | `src/schema.js` | `SETTINGS`, the known settings with their declared type and default text |
12: | `src/layer.js` | `merge`, which stacks layers so that the last one to set a key wins |
13: 
14: `test/conflayers.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the INI files the examples name.
15: 
16: ## The INI grammar
17: 
18: A line is trimmed first. An empty one, and one beginning with `#` or `;`, is ignored. `[name]` opens a section, and a section may be opened more than once. Anything else is `key = value`: the text before the first `=` is the key, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A key outside a section keeps its own name; a key inside one is prefixed with the section name and a dot, so `port` under `[server]` is `server.port`. A name and a key are one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. Nothing inside a value is special: `#` and `;` open a comment only at the start of a line.
19: 
20: ```ini
21: log.file = /var/log/app.log
22: 
23: [server]
24: port = 9090
25: ```
26: 
27: ## The schema
28: 
29: | Key | Type | Default |
30: | --- | --- | --- |
31: | `log.file` | string | (empty) |
32: | `log.level` | enum `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` | `info` |
33: | `log.rotate` | boolean | `true` |
34: | `retry.attempts` | integer | `3` |
35: | `retry.backoff` | duration | `250ms` |
36: | `server.host` | string | `localhost` |
37: | `server.port` | integer | `8080` |
38: | `server.timeout` | duration | `30s` |
39: | `server.tls` | boolean | `false` |
40: | `tags` | list | (empty) |
41: 
42: The types are declared but nothing here enforces them yet: every mode below prints the raw text as the file wrote it.
43: 
44: ## Modes
45: 
46: - `dump <file>` prints `<key>=<raw text>` for every schema key in ascending order, falling back to the schema default for a key the file leaves out. A key the schema does not know is ignored.
47: - `get <file> <key>` prints the raw text of one setting, or its default. A key outside the schema is refused.
48: 
49: ## Failures
50: 
51: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure carries the position it was read at, as `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: <message>`, where the column counts characters of the raw line from 1, leading whitespace included. The messages are `expected "]"`, reported one past the line's last non-space character; `expected a section name` and `invalid section name <name>`, at the name's first character; `expected a section header or key = value` and `invalid key <key>`, at the line's first non-space character; `expected a key`, at the `=`; and `key <key> is set twice`, at the line's first non-space character. A file that cannot be read is refused as `error: cannot read <path>`, an unknown key as `error: unknown setting <key>`, and a malformed argument list with the usage line.
52: 
53: ## Known gaps
54: 
55: Only one file is ever read, so the `merge` primitive stacks a single layer and nothing overrides anything. Nothing reads the environment. The declared types do nothing: `server.port = eighty` loads as happily as `server.port = 80`, and a caller has to coerce the text itself. `IniError` carries a position, but the parse result does not, so nothing downstream could say where a bad value was written.

(End of file - total 55 lines)

1: /** The settings this loader knows, their types, and the text each one defaults to. */
2: 
3: /** Every known setting, in ascending key order. */
4: export const SETTINGS = [
5:   { key: 'log.file', type: 'string', default: '' },
6:   { key: 'log.level', type: 'enum', members: ['debug', 'info', 'warn', 'error'], default: 'info' },
7:   { key: 'log.rotate', type: 'boolean', default: 'true' },
8:   { key: 'retry.attempts', type: 'integer', default: '3' },
9:   { key: 'retry.backoff', type: 'duration', default: '250ms' },
10:   { key: 'server.host', type: 'string', default: 'localhost' },
11:   { key: 'server.port', type: 'integer', default: '8080' },
12:   { key: 'server.timeout', type: 'duration', default: '30s' },
13:   { key: 'server.tls', type: 'boolean', default: 'false' },
14:   { key: 'tags', type: 'list', default: '' },
15: ]
16: 
17: const BY_KEY = new Map(SETTINGS.map(declared => [declared.key, declared]))
18: 
19: /**
20:  * The setting one key names, or undefined when the schema does not know it.
21:  * @param {string} key - the dotted setting key.
22:  * @returns {{key: string, type: string, members?: string[], default: string} | undefined} the setting.
23:  */
24: export function setting(key) {
25:   return BY_KEY.get(key)
26: }
27: 
28: const INTEGER = /^-?(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)$/
29: const DURATION = /^([0-9]+)(ms|s|m|h)$/
30: const UNIT_MS = { ms: 1, s: 1000, m: 60_000, h: 3_600_000 }
31: 
32: /** One value the schema refuses, worded without the position the caller adds. */
33: export class ValueError extends Error {
34:   /**
35:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
36:    */
37:   constructor(message) {
38:     super(message)
39:     this.name = 'ValueError'
40:   }
41: }
42: 
43: /** The items of a list value, trimmed, first occurrence kept. */
44: function items(declared, text) {
45:   if (text === '') return []
46:   const out = []
47:   for (const item of text.split(',')) {
48:     const trimmed = item.trim()
49:     if (trimmed === '') throw new ValueError(`${declared.key} has an empty item: ${text}`)
50:     if (!out.includes(trimmed)) out.push(trimmed)
51:   }
52:   return out
53: }
54: 
55: /**
56:  * Coerce one setting's text and render it the way `load` prints it.
57:  * @param {{key: string, type: string, members?: string[]}} declared - the setting the text belongs to.
58:  * @param {string} text - the raw text the winning layer wrote.
59:  * @returns {string} the canonical rendering.
60:  * @throws {ValueError} when the text does not fit the declared type.
61:  */
62: export function coerce(declared, text) {
63:   switch (declared.type) {
64:     case 'integer':
65:       if (!INTEGER.test(text)) throw new ValueError(`${declared.key} is not an integer: ${text}`)
66:       return text
67:     case 'boolean':
68:       if (text !== 'true' && text !== 'false') throw new ValueError(`${declared.key} is not a boolean: ${text}`)
69:       return text
70:     case 'enum':
71:       if (!declared.members.includes(text)) {
72:         throw new ValueError(`${declared.key} is not one of ${declared.members.join('|')}: ${text}`)
73:       }
74:       return text
75:     case 'duration': {
76:       const match = DURATION.exec(text)
77:       if (match === null) throw new ValueError(`${declared.key} is not a duration: ${text}`)
78:       return String(Number(match[1]) * UNIT_MS[match[2]])
79:     }
80:     case 'list':
81:       return items(declared, text).join(',')
82:     default:
83:       return text
84:   }
85: }

1: /** The environment layer: `NAME=VALUE` lines read from standard input. */
2: 
3: /** One refusal of an environment line, carrying the 1-based line and column. */
4: export class EnvError extends Error {
5:   /**
6:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line.
7:    * @param {number} column - the 1-based column of the raw line.
8:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
9:    */
10:   constructor(line, column, message) {
11:     super(message)
12:     this.name = 'EnvError'
13:     this.line = line
14:     this.column = column
15:   }
16: }
17: 
18: /** The 1-based column of the first non-space character of `raw`. */
19: function indent(raw) {
20:   return raw.length - raw.trimStart().length + 1
21: }
22: 
23: /**
24:  * The variable name one setting key travels under.
25:  * @param {string} key - the dotted setting key.
26:  * @returns {string} the variable name.
27:  */
28: export function variableName(key) {
29:   return `CONF_${key.toUpperCase().replaceAll('.', '_')}`
30: }
31: 
32: /**
33:  * Parse the environment layer.
34:  * @param {string} text - everything standard input carried.
35:  * @param {readonly {key: string}[]} settings - the schema, which decides which names are known.
36:  * @returns {Map<string, {text: string, line: number, column: number}>} each dotted key's raw value and position, in the order the input writes them.
37:  * @throws {EnvError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
38:  */
39: export function parse(text, settings) {
40:   const lines = text.split('\n')
41:   if (lines.length > 0 && lines[lines.length - 1] === '') lines.pop()
42:   const byName = new Map(settings.map(declared => [variableName(declared.key), declared.key]))
43:   const values = new Map()
44:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
45:     const line = index + 1
46:     const trimmed = raw.trim()
47:     if (trimmed === '' || trimmed.startsWith('#')) continue
48:     const split = trimmed.indexOf('=')
49:     if (split === -1) throw new EnvError(line, indent(raw), 'expected NAME=VALUE')
50:     const name = trimmed.slice(0, split).trim()
51:     if (name === '') throw new EnvError(line, indent(raw), 'expected a variable name')
52:     const key = byName.get(name)
53:     if (key === undefined) throw new EnvError(line, indent(raw), `unknown environment variable ${name}`)
54:     if (values.has(key)) throw new EnvError(line, indent(raw), `${name} is set twice`)
55:     const after = indent(raw) + split
56:     const rest = raw.slice(after)
57:     const column = rest.trim() === '' ? raw.trimEnd().length + 1 : after + (rest.length - rest.trimStart().length) + 1
58:     values.set(key, { text: rest.trim(), line, column })
59:   }
60:   return values
61: }

23: }

Everything `README.md` documents about `dump`, `get`, the INI grammar and the existing failures stays exactly as it is, including every message and every column; the work spans the parser, the schema, the layer stack, and the command.

`load <base> <site>` and `origin <base> <site>` each stack three layers, weakest first: the INI file named by the first argument, the INI file named by the second, and an environment layer read from standard input. A later layer overrides a key an earlier one set, one key at a time, so a file that sets only `server.port` leaves every other key to the layer below it. The layers are read in that order, and a layer's failures are all reported before the next layer is read.

The environment layer is a line per variable. A line is trimmed first; an empty one, and one beginning with `#`, is ignored. The rest is `NAME=VALUE`: the text before the first `=` is the name, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A setting travels under `CONF_` followed by its key uppercased with every `.` replaced by `_`, so `server.port` arrives as `CONF_SERVER_PORT`. Its failures carry a position too, worded `error: <stdin>:<line>:<column>: ` followed by `expected NAME=VALUE` or `expected a variable name` or `unknown environment variable <NAME>` or `<NAME> is set twice`, each reported at the line's first non-space character and each counting columns the way the INI parser does.

Both modes are strict about keys where `dump` is lenient: a key an INI layer sets and the schema does not know fails with `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: unknown setting <key>` at the value's position, and a layer's keys are checked in the order the file writes them, after that file parses. The value's position is the column of its first character, or, when the value is empty, one past the line's last non-space character.

`origin <base> <site>` prints `<key> <layer>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the layer is `base`, `site`, `env`, or `default` when no layer set the key.

`load <base> <site>` prints `<key>=<value>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the value is the winning layer's text coerced by the key's declared type, or the schema default coerced the same way. A `string` is its text. An `integer` is an optional `-` and then digits without a leading zero, unless the number is exactly `0`, and renders as written. A `boolean` is `true` or `false`, lowercase, and renders as written. An `enum` is one of its declared members and renders as written. A `duration` is digits followed by `ms`, `s`, `m` or `h`, and renders as its whole number of milliseconds. A `list` is items separated by commas, each trimmed, with a repeat dropped and the order kept, rendered joined by single commas; empty text is the empty list and renders empty, but an empty item between two commas is a failure. A value that does not fit its type fails with `error: <where>: <message>`, where `<where>` is the file and position it was written at, or `<stdin>` and its position when the environment layer set it, and the message is `<key> is not an integer: <text>`, `<key> is not a boolean: <text>`, `<key> is not one of <members joined by |>: <text>`, `<key> is not a duration: <text>` or `<key> has an empty item: <text>`. The keys are coerced in ascending order, so the first failing key in that order decides.

The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js dump <file>|get <file> <key>|load <base> <site>|origin <base> <site>`; `dump` takes one path, `get` a path and a key, and `load` and `origin` exactly two paths.

1: /** Link definitions: how a label is written down, normalized, and looked up. */
2: 
3: const DEFINITION = /^\[([^\]]+)\]:\s+(\S.*)$/
4: 
5: /** One refusal of a definition, carrying the 1-based line it was read at. */
6: export class RefError extends Error {
7:   /**
8:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line.
9:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
10:    */
11:   constructor(line, message) {
12:     super(message)
13:     this.name = 'RefError'
14:     this.line = line
15:   }
16: }
17: 
18: /**
19:  * One label in its comparable form: trimmed, whitespace runs collapsed, lowercased.
20:  * @param {string} label - the label as it was written.
21:  * @returns {string} the normalized label.
22:  */
23: export function normalizeLabel(label) {
24:   return label.trim().replace(/\s+/gu, ' ').toLowerCase()
25: }
26: 
27: /**
28:  * Read one line as a definition.
29:  * @param {string} raw - the line as written.
30:  * @returns {{label: string, url: string} | undefined} the definition, or undefined when the line is not one.
31:  */
32: export function readDefinition(raw) {
33:   const match = DEFINITION.exec(raw.trim())
34:   if (match === null) return undefined
35:   return { label: normalizeLabel(match[1]), url: match[2].trim() }
36: }
37: 
38: /**
39:  * Add one definition to a table, refusing a label it already holds.
40:  * @param {Map<string, {url: string, source: string}>} table - the definitions so far.
41:  * @param {number} line - the 1-based line the definition was read at.
42:  * @param {{label: string, url: string}} definition - the definition to add.
43:  * @param {string} source - the layer it came from.
44:  * @throws {RefError} when the label is already defined.
45:  */
46: export function define(table, line, definition, source) {
47:   if (table.has(definition.label)) throw new RefError(line, `label ${definition.label} is defined twice`)
48:   table.set(definition.label, { url: definition.url, source })
49: }

1: # jobq
2: 
3: A job-queue simulator with no dependencies. It reads a log from standard input and replays it on one worker against a clock that only moves when the simulation asks it to, so a run is the same on every machine and in every order.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/parse.js` | the log grammar and the refusals it words, as `LogError` |
11: | `src/queue.js` | the simulation: what starts when, and what the rate limit holds back |
12: | `src/clock.js` | `createClock`, the monotonic clock the simulation advances by hand |
13: 
14: `test/jobq.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the policy files the examples name.
15: 
16: ## The log
17: 
18: One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace. Every number is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign or a separator.
19: 
20: ```
21: limit 2 10
22: job build 5 ok
23: job flaky 3 fail ok
24: submit 0 build
25: submit 0 flaky
26: ```
27: 
28: `limit <starts> <window>` allows at most `<starts>` starts inside any window of `<window>` milliseconds, and may appear at most once. `job <id> <duration> <outcome>...` declares a job that occupies the worker for `<duration>` milliseconds and whose attempts turn out as the listed `ok` and `fail` words, the last of which repeats. An id is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. `submit <at> <id>` puts a declared job in the queue at that instant; a job may be submitted at most once.
29: 
30: ## The simulation
31: 
32: The clock starts at 0 and one worker runs everything. Take the queued attempt with the smallest ready time, breaking ties by submission order, and advance the clock to that ready time. If a rate limit is in force and the last `<starts>` starts all fall inside the window ending now, advance the clock to the instant the oldest of them leaves it. The attempt starts at the clock's instant and finishes `<duration>` later, and the clock advances to that finish. A job of duration 0 finishes in the instant it starts. A failed attempt is simply over: nothing here retries it.
33: 
34: ## Modes
35: 
36: - `trace` prints one line per attempt in the order the attempts started, `<start> <id> attempt=<n> <outcome> finish=<finish>`, and then a final `end <clock>` line.
37: - `summary` prints one line per submitted job in ascending id order, `<id> attempts=<n> <outcome of its last attempt>`, and then the same final `end <clock>` line.
38: 
39: A declared job nothing submits never runs and appears nowhere.
40: 
41: ## Failures
42: 
43: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure names its 1-based log line: `error: line 2: unknown directive cancel`. The messages are `expected limit <starts> <window>`, `expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...`, `expected submit <at> <id>`, `invalid job id <id>`, `invalid outcome <word>`, `<field> must be a non-negative integer` and `<field> must be a positive integer` naming `at`, `duration`, `starts` or `window`, `job <id> is declared twice`, `job <id> is submitted twice`, `limit is declared twice`, and `unknown directive <word>`. A `submit` line naming a job no `job` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown job <id>`. A malformed argument list is refused with the usage line.
44: 
45: ## Known gaps
46: 
47: A failure is the end of a job: there is no retry, no backoff, and nowhere for a job that never succeeds to go. The rate limit and nothing else can be configured, it can only come from the log itself, and there is no way to run the same log under a different policy.

(End of file - total 47 lines)

2:

4: const DIGITS = /^[0-9]+$/
5: 
6: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line, or 0 when the failure names none. */
7: export class LogError extends Error {
8:   /**

10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'LogError'
15:     this.line = line
16:   }
17: }
18: 
19: /**
20:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
21:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
22:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
23:  */
24: export function splitLines(text) {
25:   const split = text.split('\n')
26:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
27:   return split
28: }
29: 
30: /** One field read as a non-negative integer, or the failure that names it. */
31: function count(line, field, word) {
32:   if (!DIGITS.test(word)) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a non-negative integer`)
33:   return Number(word)
34: }
35: 
36: /** One field read as a positive integer, or the failure that names it. */
37: function positive(line, field, word) {
38:   const value = count(line, field, word)
39:   if (value < 1) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a positive integer`)
40:   return value
41: }
42: 
43: /**
44:  * Read one `limit` or `retry` line into the policy it sets.
45:  * @param {number} line - the 1-based line the directive was read at.
46:  * @param {string[]} words - the line's words.
47:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}, retry?: {max: number, base: number}}} policy - the policy so far, edited in place.
48:  * @returns {boolean} whether the directive was a policy one.
49:  * @throws {LogError} when the directive is malformed or repeated.
50:  */
51: export function policyDirective(line, words, policy) {
52:   throw new Error('not implemented')
53: }
54: 
55: /**
56:  * Parse the job log.
57:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
58:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}, retry?: {max: number, base: number}}} policy - the policy the command line already set, edited in place.
59:  * @returns {{jobs: Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>, submissions: {id: string, at: number}[]}} the declared jobs and the submissions in input order.
60:  * @throws {LogError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
61:  */
62: export function parse(lines, policy) {
63:   const jobs = new Map()
64:   const submissions = []
65:   const submitted = new Map()
66:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
67:     const line = index + 1
68:     const text = raw.trim()
69:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
70:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
71:     if (policyDirective(line, words, policy)) continue
72:     if (words[0] === 'job') {
73:       if (words.length < 4) throw new LogError(line, 'expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...')
74:       const id = words[1]
75:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
76:       if (jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is declared twice`)
77:       const duration = count(line, 'duration', words[2])
78:       for (const outcome of words.slice(3)) {
79:         if (outcome !== 'ok' && outcome !== 'fail') throw new LogError(line, `invalid outcome ${outcome}`)
80:       }
81:       jobs.set(id, { id, duration, outcomes: words.slice(3) })
82:     } else if (words[0] === 'submit') {
83:       if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected submit <at> <id>')
84:       const at = count(line, 'at', words[1])
85:       const id = words[2]
86:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
87:       if (submitted.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is submitted twice`)
88:       submitted.set(id, line)
89:       submissions.push({ id, at })
90:     } else {
91:       throw new LogError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
92:     }
93:   }
94:   for (const { id } of submissions) {
95:     if (!jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(0, `unknown job ${id}`)
96:   }
97:   return { jobs, submissions }
98: }
